title: (Scenario) Write a stored procedure that accepts two input parameters, uses them in a `WHERE` clause to fetch a value from one table into a local variable, updates a third table with that value, and returns a success status — showing parameter declaration, assigning a query result into a variable (the exact syntax is engine-specific, e.g. `SELECT ... INTO var` in PL/pgSQL & T-SQL, `SELECT col INTO var FROM ...` in Oracle PL/SQL, or `SET var = (SELECT ...)`), the update, and transactional/error handling.
shortTitle: (Scenario) Stored Procedure: Two IN Params, Fetch-Into-Variable, Update, Return Status
topicTitle: (Scenario) Write a stored procedure that accepts two input parameters, uses them

s1_definition.profdef: The task is a procedure with two IN parameters used in a `WHERE` clause to read one column from a source table into a local variable (via `SELECT ... INTO`), then use that variable to update a target table, all inside a transaction with error handling, returning a success or failure status through an OUT parameter. It demonstrates parameter declaration, assigning a single-row query result into a variable, a dependent update, and transactional and exception control.
s1_definition.analogy: A National Bank of India clerk is told an account number and a date (the two inputs). They look up that account's interest rate from the rate book (fetch one value into a note), then write that rate onto the account's ledger card (update the third table), and finally stamp the form "done" or "failed" (the status). If anything goes wrong mid-way, they tear up the partial work so the records are never left half-changed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Take two inputs, `SELECT ... INTO` a local variable from a source table, use it to `UPDATE` a target table inside a transaction with error handling, and return a success status.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The task is a procedure with two IN parameters used in a `WHERE` clause to read one column from a source table into a local variable (via `SELECT ... INTO`), then use that variable to update a target table, all inside a transaction with error handling, returning a success or failure status through an OUT parameter. It demonstrates parameter declaration, assigning a single-row query result into a variable, a dependent update, and transactional and exception control.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A National Bank of India clerk is told an account number and a date (the two inputs). They look up that account's interest rate from the rate book (fetch one value into a note), then write that rate onto the account's ledger card (update the third table), and finally stamp the form "done" or "failed" (the status). If anything goes wrong mid-way, they tear up the partial work so the records are never left half-changed.

**One line to remember:** Take two inputs, `SELECT ... INTO` a local variable from a source table, use it to `UPDATE` a target table inside a transaction with error handling, and return a success status.

sections.s2_technical:
The procedure signature declares two IN parameters and one OUT status parameter. Inside the body you declare local variables for the fetched value. You then run a single-row query using the two inputs in the `WHERE` clause and assign the chosen column into the local variable. The assignment syntax is engine-specific: Oracle PL/SQL and PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL use `SELECT col INTO var FROM ... WHERE ...`, T-SQL uses `SELECT @var = col FROM ...` (or `SET @var = (SELECT ...)`), and the portable `SET var = (SELECT ...)` subquery form works in several engines. Because the query must return exactly one row, you handle the no-row and too-many-rows cases explicitly — in Oracle these raise `NO_DATA_FOUND` and `TOO_MANY_ROWS`, and in PostgreSQL `STRICT` makes `SELECT INTO` enforce exactly one row.

With the value in the variable, you run an `UPDATE` on the target table, using the variable in the `SET` clause and the input parameters (or a key) in the `WHERE`. All of this runs inside a transaction so the read-then-update sequence is atomic. If every step succeeds you commit and set the OUT status to a success value; if any step raises an error you roll back so no partial change persists and set the status to a failure value, often also capturing the error message. The error handling block is `EXCEPTION WHEN ... THEN` in Oracle and PostgreSQL, and `BEGIN TRY / BEGIN CATCH` with `XACT_STATE()` in T-SQL.

The important correctness points to mention are: validate that exactly one source row matched before updating, check the affected row count of the `UPDATE` (via `SQL%ROWCOUNT` in Oracle, `GET DIAGNOSTICS ... ROW_COUNT` in PostgreSQL, or `@@ROWCOUNT` in T-SQL) to detect an update that matched nothing, keep the transaction short to limit lock contention, and never leave the status ambiguous — set it on both the success and the failure path. The senior nuance is that this exact pattern, read a value under a condition and apply it elsewhere atomically, is where stored procedures shine because the whole thing is one round trip and the transaction boundary is tight and local.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India needs to apply a product's current interest rate to a specific account. Given an account number and a product code (the two inputs), the procedure must look up the rate for that product from a `product_rates` table into a variable, then write that rate onto the matching row in an `account_interest` table, and return SUCCESS or a specific failure (unknown product, account not updated). The whole thing must be atomic so a lookup-then-update is never left half-applied.

Our mini-project simulates the exact procedure: declared IN params (account, product) and OUT status, a `SELECT ... INTO` of the rate from the source map, a guarded `UPDATE` of the target map using the fetched rate, transaction-style rollback on failure, and a returned status — mirroring the engine-specific SQL shown in comments.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a source table of product rates (SAV at 3.5, FD at 6.75) and a target table of account interest rates initialized to zero for A100 and A200.

Step 1 — The first call passes account A100 and product FD. The procedure runs `SELECT rate INTO v_rate` using FD in the `WHERE`, fetching 6.75 into the local variable.

Step 2 — It then updates the target table, setting A100's rate to the fetched 6.75, confirms exactly one row was affected, commits, and returns the OUT status SUCCESS with a message.

Step 3 — The second call passes product LOAN, which does not exist in the source table, so the `SELECT INTO` finds no row. The procedure treats this as the no-data case, rolls back any partial work, and returns FAILED_UNKNOWN_PRODUCT without changing the target.

Step 4 — The third call passes account A999, which does not exist in the target table, so the `UPDATE` affects zero rows. The procedure detects the zero row count, rolls back, and returns FAILED_ACCOUNT_NOT_UPDATED.

Step 5 — The final target table shows only A100 changed to 6.75, proving the dependent update applied the fetched value exactly once and both failure paths left the data untouched with a clear status.

Final output:

```text
Call 1 (A100, FD):      SUCCESS (rate 6.75 applied to A100)
Call 2 (A200, LOAN):    FAILED_UNKNOWN_PRODUCT
Call 3 (A999, SAV):     FAILED_ACCOUNT_NOT_UPDATED
Final account_interest: {A100=6.75, A200=0.0}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  CALL apply_rate(IN p_account, IN p_product; OUT p_status)
        │
        ▼ (BEGIN transaction)
  SELECT rate INTO v_rate FROM product_rates WHERE product = p_product
        │  found? ──no──▶ ROLLBACK ─▶ OUT = FAILED_UNKNOWN_PRODUCT
        │ yes (v_rate)
        ▼
  UPDATE account_interest SET rate = v_rate WHERE account = p_account
        │  rows affected? ──0──▶ ROLLBACK ─▶ OUT = FAILED_ACCOUNT_NOT_UPDATED
        │ 1 row
        ▼
  COMMIT ─▶ OUT = SUCCESS
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Fetch-Into-Variable + Dependent Update ═══

  ┌──────────────┐  CALL(acct, product)  ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ App / batch  │ ────────────────────▶ │ apply_rate procedure  │
  └──────────────┘  ◀── OUT status ────── └───────────────────────┘
                                             │ 1) SELECT INTO v_rate
                                             ▼         from product_rates (source)
                                          ┌──────────────┐
                                          │ product_rates│ (read, WHERE product=?)
                                          └──────────────┘
                                             │ 2) UPDATE using v_rate
                                             ▼
                                          ┌──────────────┐
                                          │account_interest (write, WHERE account=?)
                                          └──────────────┘
                 One transaction: all-or-nothing; status on every path.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Procedure Body & Error Handling ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Template: validate → fetch → update → commit/rollback → status    │
  │ Result Object: ProcResult carries status + message (OUT)          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: proc does one fetch-and-apply unit of work                    │
  │ O: new failure case = new guarded branch                         │
  │ D: caller depends on CALL contract + ProcResult                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── SELECT INTO syntax by engine ──
  Oracle PL/SQL : SELECT col INTO v_rate FROM t WHERE ... ; (NO_DATA_FOUND/TOO_MANY_ROWS)
  PL/pgSQL      : SELECT col INTO STRICT v_rate FROM t WHERE ... ;
  T-SQL         : SELECT @v_rate = col FROM t WHERE ... ;  or  SET @v=(SELECT ...)
  row count     : SQL%ROWCOUNT | GET DIAGNOSTICS ROW_COUNT | @@ROWCOUNT

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → call(account, product)
  3.       → SELECT INTO v_rate  [guard: no row → rollback+FAILED]
  4.       → UPDATE target       [guard: 0 rows → rollback+FAILED]
  5.       → COMMIT → OUT=SUCCESS
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
For this scenario I write a procedure with two IN parameters and an OUT status, and inside it I declare a local variable, fetch a single value into that variable using the two inputs in a `WHERE` clause, use the variable to update a third table, and wrap the whole thing in a transaction that commits on success and rolls back on any error, always setting the status. The fetch-into-a-variable step is the part whose syntax is engine-specific: Oracle PL/SQL and PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL use `SELECT col INTO v_var FROM source WHERE ...`, PostgreSQL adds `STRICT` to enforce exactly one row, T-SQL uses `SELECT @v_var = col FROM ...` or the portable `SET @v = (SELECT ...)` subquery form. Because the query must return exactly one row, I handle the no-row and too-many-rows cases explicitly — `NO_DATA_FOUND` and `TOO_MANY_ROWS` in Oracle — and after the `UPDATE` I check the affected row count with `SQL%ROWCOUNT`, `GET DIAGNOSTICS ROW_COUNT`, or `@@ROWCOUNT` to catch an update that matched nothing.

At the National Bank of India this was exactly how we applied a product's current interest rate to a specific account: the procedure took the account number and product code, did a `SELECT rate INTO v_rate FROM product_rates WHERE product = p_product`, then `UPDATE account_interest SET rate = v_rate WHERE account = p_account`, and returned SUCCESS, or a precise failure like FAILED_UNKNOWN_PRODUCT when the source lookup found nothing or FAILED_ACCOUNT_NOT_UPDATED when the update hit zero rows, rolling back so no half-applied change persisted. The correctness points I always state are to validate exactly one source row before updating, to check the update's affected row count, to keep the transaction short to limit lock contention, and to set the status on both the success and failure paths so the outcome is never ambiguous. The error block is `EXCEPTION WHEN ... THEN` in Oracle and PostgreSQL and `BEGIN TRY / BEGIN CATCH` in T-SQL. The line I always state is that you take two inputs, `SELECT ... INTO` a local variable from a source table, use it to `UPDATE` a target table inside a transaction with error handling, and return a success status.
